newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia sugar imports seen increasing.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia sugar imports seen increasing.

text.p: Indonesia's dependence on imported sugar is expected to continue, and even rise, as growing per capita incomes and an expanding population fuel consumption, industry sources said on Tuesday.

"The domestic supply side has not been able to keep pace with local consumption needs," Khor Chin Poey, president-director of PT Kerry Plantations Services Indonesia, told an international conference on sugar on the tourist island of Bali.
"This has resulted in the nation having to import about one million tonnes of sugar per annum, costing some $350 million in foreign exchange," he said.
He predicted large imports continuing in the short term and perhaps even increasing. Structural changes in the sugar industry will take time to take effect, he added.
Beddu Amang, chairman of the national logistics bureau (BULOG), said it was possible that Indonesia's annual sugar imports could touch one million tonnes.
"It is possible," he said, adding that increasing per capita incomes and an growing population were boosting consumption.
"Incomes are going up...that means consumption per person will increase," he told Reuters on the sidelines of the conference.

Indonesia was not always dependent on sugar imports. The archipelago was the world's top sugar exporter after Cuba before World War Two, with production totalling close to three million tonnes in 1930. Output in 1996 was just over two million tonnes.
The country's sugar cane industry dates back to the 17th century when the sector was initiated by the colonial Dutch government in Jakarta, then known as Batavia.
All Dutch-owned companies in Indonesia were taken over by Indonesian authorities in 1958, but sugar production never reached the heydays of the early 1930s.

"Various problems still remain such as continuing shortfall in production that leaves Indonesia a net importer," Amang told the conference, adding that problems included the inability of farmers to improve sugar cane production, and administrative snags.
Amang said the only way Indonesia could reduce sugar imports was through increased production.
"If Indonesia is to reduce its import bill while consumption continues to increase, there is only one possibility -- production must increase."
He said increased production could only come from outside the densely-populated island of Java, where land was being actively sought for industrial use and more profitable agricultural crops.

Amang said many of the sugar mills on Java were antiquated and still owned by the government. "As Indonesia enters the free trade era and proceeds with privatisation...there would appear to be little rationale for continued ownership of these aging, inefficient mills," he said.
Rante Tondok, the director-general of plantations, told the conference that future sugar mills would be constructed outside Java, with top priority given to underdeveloped eastern Indonesia.
"Investments for new sugar factories outside of Java are open for both domestic and foreign investors," he said.
He later told reporters that Indonesia's sugar output could exceed three million tonnes by the year 2005 with the opening up several new plants outside the main island of Java.
Java contributed 72 percent of total national sugar output in 1995, down from 87 percent in 1975.
